The call repeats a word the previous chapter used twice, and Ellicott hears craft, not accident, a subtle touch marking the continuity of thought; the same castaway is summoned to the highest glory and told to put on the garments of beauty belonging to her as priestly queen of cities. Henry reads the reversal as deliberate: they had asked God to awake and put on strength, and are now told to do it themselves, waking from despondency, distrust and mere dullness. He adds a caution nobody else offers: not to take irregular courses for their own relief against the law of nations concerning captives, but to use likely means of recommending themselves to the conqueror.

Then a posture that looks self-contradictory. The text has her rise and sit down, and Clarke reports the objection: sitting is the scriptural and classical attitude of mourning and agrees badly with the rising just before. His answer is furniture. Ordinary sitting in the East is on the floor with the legs crossed, on carpets or low broad couches spread with mattresses; but sitting as a posture of state is something else, a raised chair or throne with a footstool needed both to climb to it and to rest the legs once there. He quotes a traveller reporting that chairs are never used in Persia except at a coronation. Ellicott reaches the same conclusion without the ethnography: she has risen from the dust, so the sitting implies a throne, set against the seat Babylon was pushed down from.

The transaction is described twice and cancelled both times. Delitzsch explains the selling as a handing over to a foreign power from which the seller gained nothing, the object being atonement rather than profit. Ellicott makes it an answer to a complaint: the people had said in a psalm that God sold them, and the reply is that there was no real sale but a temporary transfer, so he can redeem at his own pleasure; a comparison with an earlier chapter, he adds, shows how one spiritual truth can require opposite illustrations. Gill runs the figure the other way and asks what anyone gained by selling himself to sin: not profit but loss, not liberty but bondage.

The precedents are Egypt and Assyria, and one of them raises a date. Wesley identifies the Assyrian with the king of Babylon, one empire having passed successively to Assyrians, Babylonians and Persians with the title travelling along. Ellicott allows the same wider sense and draws a conclusion: if Assyria includes Babylon here, that points to the book being written when Assyrian kings actually carried Babylon in their titles, though he thinks it likelier that the deliverance from Sennacherib is offered as a pledge of the one still to come. Both stress that neither oppression was provoked. Gill takes them as past instances confirming a redemption without money.

The last verses turn on what the oppressors are doing with their mouths. Clarke reports a hundred and twenty copies correcting a singular to a plural, and remarks that the Masoretes often kept an apparent mistake though they had evidence enough to mend it; on the verb he prefers five manuscripts and the Chaldee that make the rulers boast rather than make their captives howl, and cannot pass the word without noting that the cry it names is also the name of the Irish funeral song, and that the Arabs have one much like it. Ellicott hears God deliberating after the manner of men, asking whether the time has come to vindicate an outraged majesty. Gill has him no gainer by the captivity but a loser. On the closing promise Clarke thinks the second therefore repeated by mistake, adding no force, embarrassing the construction, and absent from the copies behind three versions. Wesley dates the knowing from the return out of Babylon, perfected at the Messiah's coming.
7:
Who the runner is depends how far forward the verse may reach. Clarke keeps it where it stands: watchmen on the mountains catch sight of a messenger bringing the long-expected news of release from Babylon, and this, he says flatly, is the literal sense. Henry narrows it, ruling out the common posts and government couriers and preferring some of the Jews themselves, near enough the fountain of intelligence to hear early and carry it. Ellicott notes the image comes from an earlier chapter, where Zion was herself the herald and the heralds now come to her. Gill will have none of the couriers, putting John the Baptist ahead of them, Christ ahead of him and the apostles after, and observing that the word for good tidings carries the sense of flesh.

Clarke stops to make a literary judgement the others do not attempt. A later prophet, he says, has manifestly taken this image, and he quotes it: behold upon the mountain the feet of the joyful messenger, celebrate thy festivals, perform thy vows. But the imitation does not equal the beauty of the original, and the subjects are not comparable, the borrower announcing only an enemy's destruction where this has something infinitely more sublime.

The next verse has a construction nobody likes. Word for word it runs, the voice of thy watchmen: they lift up their voice, and Clarke reports that neither the ancient versions nor the moderns have cleared it up naturally. He is persuaded of a mistake, two Hebrew letters being similar in sound, and would read all thy watchmen for the voice of thy watchmen, noting that in one manuscript the letter stands on an erasure; the correction perfectly rectifies sense and construction. Delitzsch keeps the text and explains the idiom: the noun with a genitive after it makes an interjectional clause and has almost become an interjection outright, so the words are simply hark, thy watchers. On seeing eye to eye, Delitzsch measures the distance at which one man looks directly into another's face, and Clarke asks whether it describes prophets and apostles, one predicting and the other finding the prediction true, the two Testaments being best understood brought face to face.

The arm comes bare next. Delitzsch supplies the gesture from the battlefield, a warrior stripping his right arm to the shoulder to fight unencumbered, and quotes a Latin poet doing the same; the arm in which holiness dwells was concealed so long that it seemed no arm at all. On the ruins told to sing, Delitzsch has the word of consolation become an act of it, the ruins shouting as they rise from the ground; Ellicott admits the return recorded in the histories looks a poor and prosaic fulfilment of so glorious a vision, and answers that the prophet idealises it and connects it, perhaps unknowingly, with another city than the earthly one. Clarke prefers a reading that puts Israel for Jerusalem, an easy slip for a scribe whose eye caught the line above.

The last order is to leave without looting. Ellicott explains that nothing unclean is to be carried off, no plunder from the fallen oppressor, only the temple vessels a Persian king restored; the bearers are Levites, though the phrase commonly means armour-bearers, which would make the whole people the great king's retinue. Wesley singles out priests and Levites and warns against carrying away superstitions with the goods. Gill hears a call out of the church of Rome, twice over, once at the Reformation and once more before the end. Delitzsch insists on the contrast with the older exodus, where the departing did enrich themselves; this is a holy procession, unstained in body and conduct. Clarke notices that a later writer turned the words inside out, giving them to the heathen as a taunt against Jews driven from Jerusalem: depart, ye are polluted, depart, forbear to touch.
13:
All of them think the chapter divided in the wrong place. Gill says a new one should begin here, these three verses treating the same subject as the next; Wesley calls it a prophecy running to that chapter's end; Ellicott puts it strongest: absolutely no connection with the verse before, and no break at the chapter's end. On who is meant, Gill catalogues what he rejects: Abraham, Moses, Ezra, Zerubbabel, any righteous man, and as leading opinions Israel in captivity, a king killed by Pharaoh, Jeremiah. He calls them weak and impertinent and turns their disagreement into an argument, men who cannot agree betraying their perplexity; the Targum, he notes, reads it of the Messiah. Henry says the same briefly, the ancient Jews taking it so and a deacon's sermon to a treasurer settling it.

Ellicott alone asks how the idea arose. He allows the revelation a starting-point in the prophet's experience: he had seen partly good kings, one nearly answering his ideal, and not one had redeemed the people; what good was done came through prophets mocked and persecuted for speaking the word. From this, he suggests, a law was dawning on him, the power of vicarious suffering and the might of martyrdom; and if such a law held, the ideal must be worked out on a wider scale, so the Servant, in all the concentric senses the word carries, the nation, its prophetic kernel, the individual identifying himself with both, must be made perfect through suffering and conquer through apparent failure.

The first promise is about outcome. Clarke translates that he shall prosper, and lays out the scheme he thinks has governed everything since the fortieth chapter: three deliverances, from Babylon, from idolatry, from sin and death, the later two shadowed under the first as under a transparent veil. Wesley keeps the word and explains its position, put first to forestall the scandal the following humiliation might cause, and counts three terms heaped up for the exaltation's height.

Then a pronoun that will not sit still. Delitzsch has the prophecy turn into direct address and sink back at once; two scholars would rather give the clause to Israel, pointed from its own degradation to the sufferings of one man, their chief reason being that a leap from second person to third is a negligence hardly imputable to the prophet; two other verses, he answers, show how little that weighs. On the marred face Clarke reports Kimchi turning it from Christ and applying it to the Jewish people, whose appearance most nations reckon unlike anyone else's; Clarke answers that the greatest kings, judges, lawgivers and poets were of Jewish extraction, Isaiah among them, and Paul, and Jesus of Nazareth. Ellicott notices how badly the verse fits the beauty Christian art made familiar, and recalls that earlier art, before Constantine, drew a worn figure with hardly any comeliness.

The last verb defeats everyone. Clarke keeps the received rendering and says at once he is by no means satisfied: the word means only to sprinkle, and the grammar wants the thing sprinkled in one case and the thing sprinkled on with a preposition, which is not what stands here. He reports Munster and two rabbis making it mean to cause speech of himself, on the analogy of dropping a word, and objects that the grammar tells against that; then a bishop's proposal that sprinkling stands for astonishing, as men are who have water thrown over them, which Clarke calls ingenious but too refined. Ellicott lists the rivals, spring up, startle, scatter, fling away, marvel at him, admits the difficulty, keeps the received text, and takes the sprinkling for a priest's cleansing of a leper by one himself counted a leper. Gill rules out baptism and prefers the doctrine, dropped like rain; Wesley agrees, the kings silent from reverence at what was strange even to Jews.
